1: They speak of an undecaying sacred fig tree with its roots above and its branches below, whose leaves are the sacred hymns. Whoever knows that tree is a knower of the Vedas.
2: Its branches spread downward and upward, grown strong by the guṇas, with the objects of sense as their shoots. And its roots stretch downward, bound up with action, in the human world.
3: Its form is not perceived here as it is, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation. This sacred fig tree, whose roots are fully grown, is to be cut down with the firm weapon of non-attachment.
4: Then that place is to be sought from which those who have gone there do not return again. And I take refuge in that very primal person, from whom the ancient activity has flowed forth.
5: Those who are without pride and delusion, who have conquered the fault of attachment, who are constant in what concerns the self, whose desires have turned away, and who are freed from the pairs called pleasure and pain: they, the undeluded, go to that undecaying place.
6: The sun does not light it up, nor the moon, nor fire. That place, from which those who have gone there do not return, is my supreme abode.
7: It is a part of me, eternal, that becomes a living being in the world of the living. It draws to itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which rest in nature.
8: When the lord takes on a body, and also when he departs from it, he goes taking these with him, as the wind takes scents from their resting place.
9: Presiding over hearing, sight and touch, taste and smell, and the mind as well, he attends on the objects of sense.
10: Whether he is departing, or staying, or experiencing, joined with the guṇas, the deluded do not see him. Those with the eye of knowledge see.
11: And the yogīs who strive see him established in the self. But the unthinking, whose self is unformed, do not see him, even though they strive.
12: The brilliance in the sun that lights up the whole world, the brilliance that is in the moon and the brilliance that is in fire: know that brilliance to be mine.
13: And entering the earth, I support beings by my vigour. And becoming the moon, whose nature is sap, I nourish all the plants.
14: Becoming the fire common to all people, I dwell in the body of breathing creatures. Joined with the outgoing and incoming breaths, I cook the four kinds of food.
15: And I am seated in the heart of all. From me come memory and knowledge, and their removal too. And I alone am what is to be known through all the Vedas. I am the maker of the end of the Vedas, and I am the knower of the Vedas as well.
16: There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable is all beings. The one who stands at the peak is called the imperishable.
17: But the highest person is another, declared to be the supreme self: the undecaying lord who enters the three worlds and sustains them.
18: Because I have gone beyond the perishable, and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the highest person.
19: Whoever, undeluded, knows me in this way as the highest person knows all, and worships me with their whole being, descendant of Bharata.
20: So I have now spoken this most secret teaching, sinless one. Whoever understands it would have buddhi, and would have done all that is to be done, descendant of Bharata.
